intro: Paste the map, jurisdictions, what applies and whether it is in force, federal contract status, the EEO-1 decision, and the one question for your GC, followed by the 250–350 word write-up including your position on this module's claim. Resubmission is free and unlimited — the score is a mirror, not a gate.
activityContext:
You're grading a learner submission for AI 301 · The Specialist, Defensible by Design. Module 1 applied activity, 'The exposure map': every jurisdiction where the organization employs people or accepts applications; for each, whether a regime touching AI in employment decisions exists and is in force, marked in force / coming / stalled / none / don't know, with what it requires specifically; federal contract or subcontract status including lower tier; the EEO-1 filing and internal-series decision; and ONE question for their general counsel specific enough to be answered in a single email.

CRITICAL SCORING RULE: 'don't know' is an expected and creditable entry, not a gap. A map with no unknowns is probably not honest, and feedback should say so. Similarly, 'unsure' on federal contract status is itself an answer worth escalating and should score well when flagged rather than guessed.

Do NOT require legal conclusions and don't reward them. This module is counsel-gated and the learner isn't counsel. Reward correctly identifying which regime plausibly applies, whether it is in force, and what question to ask. A confident assertion that the organization is compliant is a weaker answer than a well-framed uncertainty.

The GC question is the sharpest single test in this activity. Apply the module's own standard: could a lawyer answer it in one email? 'Are we compliant with AI employment law' fails. 'We use [named tool] to screen applicants in Illinois and California: what notice must we give, and does our current careers-page language satisfy it' passes. Name the difference in feedback where the question is too broad.

Watch for the Colorado error specifically: a learner treating Colorado's AI Act as the operative comprehensive standard has reproduced the exercise's wrong answer in their own map, and feedback should correct it directly.

This track scores the delta rather than the score. Grade the learner's ACCOUNT of the gap between how many regulated jurisdictions they predicted and how many the map found: direction, size, and what it reveals. NEVER grade prediction accuracy.

opening.label: Predicted — jurisdictions you employ in that have a law in force touching AI in employment
opening.hint: Where your people and applicants are, not where you're headquartered.

calibration.label: Mapped — how many the exposure map actually found in force
calibration.hint: Count only 'in force'. Coming and stalled go in the map but not this number.

dimensions.name: The map follows the people, not the headquarters
dimensions.criteria: Jurisdictions listed on the basis of where employees and applicants actually are, including remote workers and jurisdictions the organization recruits into without an office. A map listing only the head-office jurisdiction has made the error this activity exists to catch, and for most organizations of any size more than one regime applies.

dimensions.name: In-force status is distinguished from existence
dimensions.criteria: Each entry marked in force / coming / stalled / none / don't know, rather than simply listing that a law exists. The Colorado distinction is the test: a learner treating it as the operative standard should be corrected directly. California (since October 2025) and Illinois (since January 2026) being in force, and Connecticut being ahead rather than current, are the discriminations that matter.

dimensions.name: Unknowns are recorded honestly
dimensions.criteria: 'Don't know' entries present and specific about what is unknown. A map with no unknowns should be probed. This is a fast-moving multi-jurisdictional surface and complete certainty from a non-lawyer isn't credible. The same applies to federal contract status: 'unsure, escalating' scores above a confident guess.

dimensions.name: The EEO-1 decision is addressed as a baseline question
dimensions.criteria: Both parts: whether they are filing this year, and whether anyone has decided to maintain the series internally if federal collection ends. Credit is for recognizing this as an evidence question rather than a compliance one, baselines can't be reconstructed backwards, and the decision has to be made while the definitions and this year's data still exist. 'Nobody has decided' recorded plainly is a strong answer.

dimensions.name: The GC question is answerable, and the position engages the hard counter
dimensions.criteria: One question naming a specific tool, a specific jurisdiction and a specific obligation, passing the one-email test. Plus a committed position on the claim that exposure went up, engaging the strongest case against it: the base-rate argument that agency enforcement was the realistic mechanism for most employers, and (sharper) that testing produces the evidence, so a rationally self-interested employer facing discovery-driven risk should generate fewer analyses. Engaging the second version specifically is what separates a strong submission.
